newsitem.title: GERMANY: Gaddum - Buba may free repos from minimum reserves.
newsitem.headline: Gaddum - Buba may free repos from minimum reserves.

text.p: The Bundesbank is likely to free securities repurchase, or repo, business from minimum reserve requirements, the bank's deputy president told a German newspaper.
In an interview with the Boersen-Zeitung published on Tuesday, Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said such a decision was up to the central bank's policy-making council, of which he is a member.
But he said he was confident that the council would decide this autumn to exempt repo business from minimum reserves, the newspaper said.

Germany's minimum reserve requirement is widely perceived as a burden on the financial centre which has prompted banks to shift their repurchase business in German securities from Frankfurt to London.
In Germany, banks must deposit a certain percentage of short-term borrowings from foreign banks and domestic non-banks in non-interest bearing deposits at the Bundesbank.
Currently the level on repo business and sight deposits is two percent, and 1.5 percent on savings deposits.

Under a repo transaction, a dealer borrows funds from an investor by selling securities to him. The dealer repurchases the securities at a later date, thereby repaying the loan. The difference between the sale and repurchase price represents interest on the loan.

Boersen-Zeitung said the Bundesbank had conducted a detailed survey among banks this year to find out the size of bank's domestic and foreign repo business and what impact an exemption for repos would have on the minimum reserves.
Recent comments from Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick had created the impression that the Bundesbank objections to an exemption for repos had strengthened, the paper said.
Gaddum wanted to counter that impression, but he declined to reveal the findings of the survey, the paper said.
He said one should expect "no wonders" from the exemption and that repo business currently done in London would probably not be shifted back to Frankfurt.

Gaddum said the survey was intended to find out whether the exemption would affect the "substance of the minimum reserve" and stressed that the Bundesbank had never left any doubt that that substance should be maintained as it remained necessary.
